canberra.snippet: A major highway has been shut in both directions in southern NSW after a horror multi-vehicle crash. A NSW Police spokesperson said that ...
canberra.content:
21 September 2026

Start the conversation

The horror crash has closed the Princes Highway near Bodalla. Image: LiveTraffic NSW.

A major highway has been shut in both directions in southern NSW after a horror multi-vehicle crash.

A NSW Police spokesperson said that at about 2 pm today (21 September), emergency services were called to Princes Highway at Bodalla, near Brou Lake Road, following reports of a crash.

Officers from South Coast Police District attended and found a car and a motorcycle had collided.

The rider of the motorcycle died at the scene.

While yet to be formally identified, police believe he is a man in his 70s.

The driver of the car – a 38-year-old man – was treated by NSW Ambulance paramedics.

He was airlifted to hospital for further treatment and mandatory testing.

Police have established a crime scene and begun an investigation into the crash.

As of 4 pm today, the Princes Highway is currently closed in both directions 2.5 km north of Brou Tip Road.

According to a Live Traffic NSW alert, motorists are advised to delay non-essential travel.

Light vehicles can use the following diversions:

  • Northbound travel: Snowy Mountains Highway, Monaro Highway, Numeralla Road, Cooma St, Countegany Road, Badja Road, Krawarree Road, Cooma Road, Kings Highway and Princes Highway
  • Southbound travel: Kings Highway, Cooma Road, Krawarree Road, Badja Road, Countegany Road, Cooma Street, Numeralla Road, Monaro Highway, Snowy Mountains Highway and Princes Highway.

Live Traffic warns that heavy vehicles will be parked.

A report will be prepared for the coroner.

As inquiries continue, anyone with information, including dashcam footage, is urged to contact Crime Stoppers on 1800 333 000.

canberra.title: $500,000 rewards aim to solve five Canberra cold cases that haunt their families
canberra.snippet: A suspected murder, a suspicious disappearance, a fatal hit-and-run and two women who vanished without a trace. These descriptions relate...
canberra.content:
The deaths or disappearances of these five people remain unsolved (clockwise from top left): Keren Rowland, Megan Louise Mulquiney, Troy Hugh Forsyth, Elizabeth Herfort and David Abuoi. Photos: ACT Policing.

A suspected murder, a suspicious disappearance, a fatal hit-and-run and two women who vanished without a trace.

These descriptions relate to five different people who all have three factors in common, including that they are unsolved cold cases in Canberra and have left behind devastated families haunted by not knowing what happened to their loved ones.

Police are now hoping to provide the families with answers after the ACT Government announced $500,000 rewards for information on each of their disappearances or deaths.

“The families of these five people have never given up hope of getting answers regarding what happened to their loved ones,” Minister for Police Marisa Paterson said.

“We hope that by offering these rewards, there is a significant incentive for people with information to come forward and tell police what they know.”

The rewards are for information on the murder of Keren Rowland in 1971, the disappearances of Elizabeth Herford in 1980 and Megan Mulquiney in 1984, the fatal hit-and-run of Troy Forsyth in 1987, and the disappearance of David Abuoi in 2012.

ACT Chief Police Officer Scott Lee said ACT Policing’s Unsolved Homicide and Long-Term Missing Persons Team identified these five cases as the most likely to have witnesses or information that could assist investigators.

As a result of this review, police asked the ACT Government to consider making the rewards.

“One small piece of information may be all that’s required to lead us to the answers that we seek,” Mr Lee said.

Troy Forsyth’s sister Vanessa Forsyth (centre) speaks to media with Chief Police Officer Scott Lee and Minister for Police Marisa Paterson. Photo: Albert McKnight.

Troy Forsyth’s sister, Vanessa Forsyth, thanked the government for releasing the “huge” reward for information into her 17-year-old brother’s death.

“I’m hoping, after such a long time, that this may encourage someone to come forward,” she said.

“[My brother’s death] has had a significant impact on my family, but not only to me, it’s passed down onto my children as well.

“I’ll never stop until we get answers.”

Elizabeth Herfort’s family said her mother and father had both died waiting for news of her.

“Since Elizabeth’s disappearance, we’ve led lives of profound grief and the dawning awareness that she was the best of us,” the family said in a statement.

“We simply ask if anyone remembers or knows anything that may be helpful in finding her, or finding out what happened to her, to please contact the police.”

Megan Mulquiney’s mother, Dorothy Tallis, said 42 years was a long time to carry a secret.

“People grow older. Circumstances change. Relationships and loyalties change. What may have felt impossible to say in 1984 may be possible to say today,” she said.

“If you have protected somebody else, please think about the family that has spent more than four decades without Megan.

“This is Megan. She was 17. She mattered then, and she matters just as much today.”

These five new rewards are the first to be announced in the ACT for 14 years.

In 2012, $500,000 rewards had been announced for information into the unsolved murders of Kathryn Grosvenor in 2002, Susan Winburn in 2004 and Frank Campbell in 2005.

These three cases remain unsolved.

Minister for Police Marisa Paterson and Chief Police Officer Scott Lee address media about the rewards. Photo: Albert McKnight.

There are two other unsolved deaths of children in the ACT: six-year-old Allen Redston in 1966 and two-year-old Safa Annour in 2018.

Detective Sergeant Craig Marriott said Safa’s death remained under investigation by the homicide team, but police did not feel a reward for information into her death was necessary at this point in time.

“Whilst [Allen Redston’s death] remains an open investigation, there’s no active lines of inquiry being pursued at the moment,” he said.

“As much and as eager as we are to solve Allen Redston’s murder, the age of that makes it very, very difficult. And certainly the opportunities for information to be provided in that are dwindling with time.”

In 2012, a reward was announced for information relating to the 1999 murder of Irma Palasics. Two men were eventually sentenced over her death earlier this year after the case was solved thanks to the National DNA Database.

Detective Marriott said the reward strategy was still successful, as it led to an influx of information about Mrs Palasics’ death.

“As a strategy, yes, putting up a reward is absolutely of assistance to police. As to whether it provides that key piece of information that leads to a prosecution, let’s wait and see,” he said.

The five new $500,000 rewards are for information that leads to the successful prosecution of the person or people responsible for the unsolved homicide or missing persons cases.

If you have information about any of these unsolved cases, provide your contact details to Crime Stoppers.

canberra.title: Elderly mobility scooter rider dies after crash in north Canberra
canberra.snippet: A 95-year-old man has died a week after he was hit by a car while riding his mobility scooter in northern Canberra. An ACT Policing spoke...
canberra.content:
An investigation is underway after an elderly man died a week after a crash in Bruce. Photo: Michelle Kroll.

A 95-year-old man has died a week after he was hit by a car while riding his mobility scooter in northern Canberra.

An ACT Policing spokesperson said a white Toyota Alphard van collided with a blue mobility scooter at the intersection of Ginninderra and Haydon Drives in Bruce at around 11 am on 13 September 2026.

The elderly man who had been riding the scooter and the 47-year-old female driver of the van were both taken to hospital with minor injuries.

However, the man’s condition deteriorated and he died on Sunday (20 September).

“This is the 12th death on ACT roads this year,” the police spokesperson said.

“ACT Road Policing’s Major Collision Team is investigating the circumstances surrounding the collision.

“A report will be prepared for the coroner.”

If you saw this crash or have dash-cam footage, contact Crime Stoppers ACT. Quote reference number 8497963.

The Toyota van had ACT registration YRQ 96X.

canberra.title: More Aussies dying than being born by 2060s, says Intergenerational Report
canberra.snippet: There will be more Australians dying than being born in the 2060s and by then artificial intelligence will have dramatically changed the ...
canberra.content:
Treasurer Jim Chalmers has delivered his second Intergenerational Report. Image: Screenshot.

There will be more Australians dying than being born in the 2060s and by then artificial intelligence will have dramatically changed the economy.

That’s the takeaway from the latest Intergenerational Report, released on Monday (21 September) by Treasurer Jim Chalmers during a speech at Australian National University.

The report, prepared by Treasury, outlines the challenges Australia will face over the next four decades, and it presents starker changes than previously forecast.

“No previous IGR has contended with global challenges this great, with politics this fraught, or a future less certain,” the Treasurer said.

“The global and generational risks are serious, but Australia’s opportunities are endless,” the Treasurer said.

Australia’s population will keep ageing due to falling fertility rates and the fact that, for the first time, deaths are projected to outnumber births over the next 40 years.

Numerous advanced economies, such as Germany, Japan, and South Korea, have already reached that milestone, and most others are likely to follow in the coming decades.

Fertility in Australia is expected to fall to 1.34 children per woman by 2065, while the number of Australians over 85 will triple by 2066.

The report states that five major transitions are underway in the global economy, with “profound implications” for Australia’s economy, budget and society.

These include AI developing rapidly to be a defining influence on the economy over the next 40 years.

Geopolitical fragmentation is also increasing as conflict and competition have flared and broadened.

The third transition is energy becoming more important and urgent, and the fourth is the population ageing more quickly.

Lastly, Australia’s industrial base is evolving further towards services, influenced by AI and the other major transitions.

It is Australia’s seventh Intergenerational Report (IGR), and the second to be delivered by Dr Chalmers.

He said the report shows risks to Australia’s economy and pressures on the budget are serious, but the country’s advantages are substantial.

“The report confirms Australia is better placed and better prepared to deal with rapid change than most countries, but despite our advantages we cannot be complacent,” the Treasurer said.

“This IGR’s projections show that in 2066, Australians are expected to live longer, healthier lives, with higher living standards and more secure retirements.

“At the same time, families will have fewer kids, the population will grow more slowly, and our industries will be transformed by artificial intelligence and clean energy.

“Advances in AI represent the most dramatic change since the last IGR in 2023, and we’re acting now to maximise the opportunities and minimise the serious risks it presents.”

The underlying cash balance is projected to improve over the medium term, to a deficit of 0.3 per cent of GDP in 2036–37, then widen over the long term to reach a deficit of 1.8 per cent of GDP in 2065–66.

This is an improvement of 1.2 percentage points of GDP in 2062–63, compared to the 2023 IGR.

Gross debt as a share of GDP is projected to decline to 22.2 per cent in the mid‑2050s before increasing to 27.4 per cent by 2065–66 – is an improvement of 7.2 percentage points of GDP in 2062–63, compared to the 2023 IGR.

Younger Australians, however, will be working longer and will find it difficult to buy a home without the same early income gains experienced by earlier generations.

“As the population ages, increased demand for care and support services will reinforce shifts in the economy towards services,” the IGR states.

“This long-run trend towards services and the care economy will coincide with the adoption and diffusion of AI and broader changes in the industrial base.

“Against this backdrop, intergenerational equity is being strained by the long-term decline in home ownership and the pressures that an ageing population and structural trends in the tax base are placing on working-age Australians.

“Democracies around the world are also under increasing pressure as economic anxieties lead to fracturing and fragmentation. Discontent is driving political upheaval at faster rates than in recent decades.

“This underscores the urgency of governments responding to the real pressures and concerns in the community through ambitious reform and long-term planning.”

With weaker productivity growth accompanying the ageing population, and rising defence and health costs thrown in, it all adds up to increasing pressure on government finances.

Real GDP per person will expand by about 1.2 per cent over the next 40 years, down from 1.5 per cent over the previous four decades.

Dr Chalmers said the report “makes the case” for the Federal Government’s “ambitious reform agenda” to boost productivity and resilience.

He said the IGR justifies Labor’s housing tax changes in the last federal budget.

“In all the 20 or so budgets that I’ve worked on or responded to in my time in politics, there hasn’t been a budget that has been more serious about meeting our intergenerational obligations,” he said.

“And I think the pointiest part of that, the defining part of that, is really the housing market, which has locked young people out for too long.”

canberra.title: Canberra strata meetings to get easier as new bill clears way for rental gas phase-out
canberra.snippet: Canberra apartment owners could find it easier to make decisions at strata meetings, while landlords would have fewer hurdles to replacin...
canberra.content:
Attorney General Tara Cheyne has introduced the Housing and Consumer Affairs Legislation Amendment Bill 2026. Photo: Michelle Kroll.

Canberra apartment owners could find it easier to make decisions at strata meetings, while landlords would have fewer hurdles to replacing gas appliances with electric ones under new laws introduced in the ACT Legislative Assembly.

Attorney General Tara Cheyne introduced the Housing and Consumer Affairs Legislation Amendment Bill 2026, which makes changes across strata properties, rental homes, retirement villages and land title caveats.

Ms Cheyne described it as an “unassuming” bill but said it contained some significant reforms. Another bill is expected early next year covering occupancy agreements and further changes to residential tenancy laws.

One of the biggest changes is for owners corporations, where getting enough owners to attend meetings can be difficult.

The bill would cut the quorum needed for a general meeting from 50 per cent of eligible voters to 25 per cent, including for unit-titled retirement villages.

The change follows recommendations from the Legislative Assembly’s inquiry into the management of strata properties.

Property Council ACT and Capital Region executive director Ashlee Berry said lowering the threshold could make it easier for owners corporations to get things done.

“Lowering the owners corporation quorum could help overcome persistent difficulties getting enough owners to meetings, but it must be backed by strong notice, voting and transparency safeguards,” she said.

The bill would also remove the current reduced-quorum petition process and the 28-day wait before decisions made at those meetings take effect. Instead, a decision could take effect the next day.

That could help owners corporations act faster on urgent repairs, legal action or other time-sensitive matters.

Owners who disagree with a decision could still take the matter to the ACT Civil and Administrative Tribunal (ACAT), without first having to organise a petition of other owners. The bill would also clarify how proxy and absentee votes count towards a quorum.

The legislation also makes changes for Canberra renters as the ACT moves away from gas.

At the moment, landlords are required to maintain utility connections, including gas. The bill would remove that requirement once there are no gas appliances left in a rental property.

If a landlord chooses to disconnect the gas, they would have to pay the cost.

The bill also deals with what happens when a landlord replaces a gas appliance with an electric one.

Tenants can currently seek a rent reduction if the loss or reduced use of an appliance affects their use and enjoyment of the property.

Under the changes, they would not be able to claim a rent reduction simply because a gas appliance had been replaced with a reasonable electric alternative.

Ms Berry said the changes appeared practical as long as renters were not left worse off.

“The proposed gas changes also appear pragmatic where landlords cover the disconnection cost and tenants receive a genuinely reasonable electric replacement,” she said.

Real Estate Institute of ACT CEO Maria Edwards also backed the change, saying it made sense as Canberra moved towards electrification.

But she said converting rental properties could come at a significant cost to landlords once the cost of new cooking, hot water and heating appliances, installation and qualified tradespeople was taken into account.

Ms Edwards said tenants should benefit from improved energy efficiency and lower utility costs as households moved away from gas, making the removal of the right to seek a rent reduction simply because an appliance had been substituted fair.

However, she warned there could be disputes over exactly what counted as a “reasonable” replacement.

“A grey area will be the determination of ‘reasonable’ and ‘like for like’ in substituting appliances such as heating – if a property currently has ducted heating will this need to be replaced with ducted electric heating, or will split systems suffice – and how many?” she said.

“Expectations between landlords and tenants can often diverge when there are grey areas such as these.”

Tenants could still seek a rent reduction through ACAT if there was no active electricity connection or the landlord’s actions were unreasonable or impractical.

The Property Council broadly supports the direction of the bill, saying reforms that make strata decisions easier, support electrification and reduce regulatory duplication were welcome.

There are also changes for retirement villages.

Currently, each village operator must set up an internal disputes committee made up of an operator representative, a resident and an independent chair.

Ms Cheyne said the system had been difficult to make work. Some villages had been unable to establish a committee, while residents could be reluctant to get involved in disputes between neighbours and friends.

The bill would remove the requirement to have a committee, although villages could keep one if residents and operators wanted it.

Residents would still be able to take disputes to the ACT Human Rights Commission or ACAT, and operators could not put terms in contracts forcing residents to use a particular dispute process.

The bill also makes a smaller change for people lodging caveats over ACT land.

They would no longer need an ACT address for official notices and could provide an address anywhere in Australia. They could also nominate an email address.

The bill has been introduced but is yet to pass the Assembly, with debate to continue at a later sitting.

australia.title: Boy, 11, in serious condition after being shot in face and neck in Sydney home
australia.snippet: Three 18-year-old men were arrested at the unit in Norwest, police said, but officers played down link to organised crime Get our breakin...
australia.content:
An 11-year-old boy has been taken to hospital in a serious condition after being shot in a home in Sydney’s north-west.

The child was receiving life-saving treatment in hospital on Monday night after suffering gunshot wounds to his face and neck, police said.

He was found injured at about 5pm at a unit on Fairway Drive, Norwest, after emergency services arrived in response to reports of a shooting at the property.

Paramedics treated the boy at the scene before taking him to hospital.

Initial reports indicated the shots were fired from within the home.

Speaking a few hours after the incident, Supt Naomi Moore said four 18-year-old men and a 44-year-old woman had been inside the unit at the time, all of whom were unharmed and were assisting with the investigation.

Three of the 18-year-olds had been arrested, Moore said.

Moore said while the investigation was just starting, police had no information to suggest the incident was related to organised crime.

There have been at least six suspected mistaken-identity shootings in Sydney since the start of last year.

Last week, two teenage boys were charged with murder after the recent shooting death of a university student in Sydney, which police say was a case of mistaken identity.

Moore assured people in the community who were “fearful on the streets at the moment” that police did not believe Monday’s shooting in Norwood was related to organised crime.

Police were investigating how the gun came to be in the house, as there were no firearms registered to that address, she said.

Moore said she was not sure what type of gun had been used, or where the weapon was located.

“In terms of what happened in that apartment, it is far too early for me to say right now,” she said.

“[But] we have all sorts of resources down there … to ensure that we do get to the bottom of what happened in that unit tonight.”

Police had established an “expansive” crime scene as investigations into the incident continued.

“It’s a tragic situation with an 11-year-old child suffering this injury,” Moore said.

“The mother is with the child at the moment – she is as distressed as any parent would be about what she is dealing with at the moment.”

australia.title: Think Australia would be better off with less migration? The numbers tell a different story
australia.snippet: The population is ageing and we’re having fewer babies. Labor should keep that in mind as the migration debate rages Get our new politica...
australia.content:
The intergenerational report lays bare how today’s growing anti-migration rhetoric clashes with a future where we need to attract people from overseas to help grow the economy and pay for our ageing population.

The “replacement” fertility rate is 2.1 children per woman – this is the average number of births to keep the population steady without migration and we’ve been below this level for 50 years.

The fertility rate is about 1.5 now and the IGR projects it will drop to 1.34 over the coming 40 years. This is how Treasury makes the alarming prediction that by the mid-2060s deaths will outnumber births for the first time.

There is no direct plan to reverse the trend for smaller Australian families, and Chalmers has made it clear Labor has no intention of repeating Peter Costello’s baby bonus or the former Liberal treasurer’s free advice on how many babies we should be having.

“When it comes to fertility rates, I do not and will not give people free advice about these very personal decisions that they make about whether to start a family and when to start a family,” the treasurer said on Monday.

Fair enough, but the seventh IGR tells a very familiar story that Australians are, on average, getting older – and this has big implications for the economy and the budget.

It means there is a smaller share of workers paying the taxes to fund the growing burden of paying for things associated with an ageing population, like healthcare and aged care.

Maintaining a healthy migration program has helped – and will help – Australia overcome these structural challenges.

As the IGR says: “Migration contributes to population growth and slows ageing, while supporting a multicultural society and strengthening the economy through skills, innovation and international connections.”

For those who think we would be better off with less migration, Treasury’s analysis provides some evidence that the opposite is true.

The IGR’s “baseline forecast” assumes a long-run net overseas migration (Nom) figure of 235,000 people a year.

This central case predicts real GDP per person – a reasonable proxy for average living standards – to grow from $99,200 in this financial year, to $157,300 in 40 years’ time.

Treasury economists then ran the numbers under a lower population scenario, where Nom was 50,000 a year less, and where the long-run fertility rate was 1.24, instead of 1.34.

Under this scenario, real GDP per person would be $400 lower in 2065-66 than under the baseline.

That’s not much, but it’s working in the wrong direction.

The impacts of lower population growth are more stark when it comes to forecasts of what’s known as the “dependency ratio”.

In 2025-26, there will be 27.4 people aged 65 and over for every 100 working-age Australians. The IGR projects this ratio will soar to 40 by the mid-2060s; with lower migration it reaches 43.

That hits the budget.

The projected underlying cash deficit with lower population growth is 2.4% in 2065-66, instead of 1.8% under the existing assumptions.

Gross debt as a share of GDP is nearly 10 percentage points higher, at 32.2%.

These are the numbers that any responsible government has to keep in mind when trying to navigate its way safely through the shoals of migration politics.

australia.title: Rebel Wilson back in court as The Deb producers sue star over allegedly blocking film
australia.snippet: Hollywood actress appears in NSW supreme court in Sydney for the latest lawsuit over her directorial debut Get our breaking news email , ...
australia.content:
Hollywood star Rebel Wilson had a “last chance” phone call with her film’s co-producers over a dispute about up-front costs and her $1m fee, a judge has heard.

The Pitch Perfect and Bridesmaids star appeared in the New South Wales supreme court in Sydney on Monday in the latest lawsuit over her directorial debut, a musical comedy named The Deb.

The film’s release was shelved in 2024 after Wilson fell out with co-producers.

Vince Holden, Gregor Cameron and Amanda Ghost claim Wilson and her company, Camp Sugar, breached consumer law concerning misleading conduct and breached various contracts when making allegedly defamatory statements about them to her 11 million Instagram followers in July 2024.

The producers claimed Wilson accused them of inappropriate conduct toward the lead actor in the film, embezzling funds and trying to block its release.

Wilson was accused of preventing the release by undermining negotiations with potential distributors and threatening an injunction against showing the film in Australia.

In a cross-claim, Wilson and Camp Sugar allege Ghost, Cameron and Holden’s involvement in the film was marked by “a troubling pattern of illicit egregious behaviours, including theft, bullying and sexual misconduct”.

Wilson claimed Ghost broke verbal agreements over writing credits and a soundtrack album deal and Cameron and Holden embezzled $900,000 from a joint venture company set up to make the film.

Wilson sat in the back row of the small courtroom, frequently typing on her phone, as her barrister, Dauid Sibtain SC, questioned one of the film’s producers.

Holden, part of AI Film Production Limited, which brought the lawsuit, was asked about a series of budget and financing emails regarding the 2024 film.

Holden agreed he asked for a “last-chance call” in October 2023 over AI Film’s requests for increased fees and Wilson’s offer to reduce her acting and directing fee to $1m.

Sibtain asked if Wilson had been incredibly upset and angry at AI Film’s proposed $300,000 fee rising to more than $650,000 plus finance costs without consulting her.

“I would not say upset,” Holden said.

“She didn’t like the fees being there.”

After he cut off further money towards the film, Holden told fellow producers: “the clock has stopped ticking and I’m waiting for the boom.”

“AI Film had advanced considerable funds to keep the production on time and we didn’t have a final agreement on fee levels,” he said.

AI Film had planned an “extremely bold investment” toward producing The Deb before securing a share of the rights to the film.

“You accepted that $15m was a lot of money to risk on a first-time director, do you agree?” Sibtain asked.

“Correct, yes,” Holden said.

Holden agreed AI Film was “quite content to risk that money and see where it ended up” and that the risk increased when the budget “subsequently went up to over $20m”.

AI Film company directors claimed these alleged statements breached contracts and Wilson’s obligations as production company director.

That allegedly caused economic loss, a potential film distributor to withdraw an offer and reputational damage to the producers.

Wilson and her company had an initial fee of six per cent of the film’s budget, shared 50-50 with AI Film.

The Deb – eventually released in April 2026 – had multiple estimates for its potential worldwide revenue, starting from a predicted loss of $4.5m if it performed poorly.

If successful, the film could “break even” or make a multimillion-dollar profit, Justice Elisabeth Peden heard.

As a musical comedy with an Australian theme, The Deb’s predicted revenue was based on films Pitch Perfect, Muriel’s Wedding, The Adventures of Priscilla, Queen of the Desert and Strictly Ballroom.

“They were all breakout successes but some of them came out 15 to 30 years ago,” Sibtain said.

“When people went to cinemas, before streaming.”

The hearing continues.

The equity case comes after a blockbuster defamation trial in May involving Wilson and the star of her directorial debut.

Australian actor Charlotte MacInnes claimed she was defamed in four social media posts by Wilson but a judge in July dismissed the case.

australia.title: Universal early childhood education better than baby bonus to increase Australia’s birthrate, Labor says
australia.snippet: Intergenerational report predicts that in four decades’ time, more Australians will be dying than being born each year Get our breaking n...
australia.content:
Labor says better investment in early childhood education and care, such as a possible move to universal access for families, is a better way to address Australia’s declining birthrate, rejecting the need for a new “baby bonus”.

Monday’s intergenerational report showed that more Australians will be dying than being born in 40 years’ time, a point already reached by countries including South Korea, Italy, Germany and Japan.

It is the first time the three-yearly report has forecast more deaths than births.

Lower fertility rates will drive slower population growth, according to Treasury’s report. Australia’s fertility rate is projected to decline to 1.34 by 2065–66, down from 1.5 children per woman in 2030–31.

Fertility rates have been below the replacement rate of 2.1 children per woman for 50 years, contributing to a projected drop in population of 1.7 million people and an increase in the projected median age by 1.7 years in 2065–66.

The report says a complex mix of economic, social and cultural factors is to blame, including greater access to contraception, more time spent in education, career development, longer periods living with parents, and delays in forming partnerships and having children.

The treasurer, Jim Chalmers, said fewer families with more than three children was part of the drop.

“When it comes to fertility rates, I do not and will not give people free advice about these very personal decisions that they make about whether to start a family and when to start family,” he said.

He said federal Labor was making it easier for adults to choose to have more children if they wished, citing expanded paid parental leave, superannuation settings and access to childcare.

The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, wants universal childcare to be part of his political legacy, and the government has commissioned consulting giant Deloitte to help design a universal system. Its report on the policy “pathway” is due in time for the next election.

The assistant minister for productivity, Andrew Leigh, said the government would “prefer that it were otherwise, but that’s the norm around the world.”

“My read of the evidence, as an economist, is that the biggest impact you have is around childcare, and that’s why we made it such a priority upon coming to government, improving access to childcare, ensuring that it is affordable for Australians.”

But, Liberal frontbencher Andrew Hastie said he was “open minded” about an economic incentive, like a return to the Howard government’s baby bonus payment.

“The real problem is of course that family formation is being delayed because people can’t get into home soon enough, and families are having less children,” he told ABC TV.

“We want Australians to have a better chance of getting into a home, forming a family and having children of their own.”

The Nationals leader, Matt Canavan, said families should have more support, but a baby bonus payment was not the right approach.

He has previously called for a “hyper” Australia and “more Australian babies”. He said solutions should be designed around helping families working for their own advancement.

“The baby bonus, it was just ‘Here’s some cash’, without you having to put in the effort as well.”

Research by the e61 thinktank found that the baby bonus, introduced by then treasurer Peter Costello in 2004, led to births increasing by 6.5%. Births increased by 10% among mothers with no taxable income, by 8% among below-median income mothers, while there was no change among high-income mothers. It also found that births of a third child increased by 9%, and that mothers who received the baby bonus, as a group, had 6.8% more children in total by 2022.

The finance minister, Katy Gallagher, said the government would not revisit the baby bonus.

“Our government doesn’t get into promoting choices for individual families, but we recognise that people making those choices should be supported.”

australia.title: Hastie ‘open minded’ on return of baby bonus to counter ageing population concerns – as it happened
australia.snippet: This blog is now closed Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Dan Tehan says fuel excise cut when oil price high a...
australia.content:
Andrew Hastie ‘open minded’ on return to baby bonus after report’s warning about ageing population

Andrew Hastie has weighed in on the latest intergenerational report, saying he’s “open minded” on government financial incentives to encourage people to have children.

The report, released earlier today, found there will be more Australians dying than being born in 40 years’ time, and examines the fundamental challenges of managing an ageing population at a time of rapid change and lower economic growth.

It also outlines how Australia is at the cusp of a new and uncertain age of artificial intelligence that will shape the economy and society over the coming four decades.

Hastie was interviewed on the ABC’s Afternoon Briefing program a short time ago, where he said:

“The real problem is of course that family formation is being delayed because people can’t get into home soon enough, and families are having less children.

“It is a real concern that our fertility replacement rate is projected to drop further, to a historic low at the moment of about 1.39 I think it was, and we want Australians to have a better chance of getting into a home, forming a family and having children of their own.”

Asked if he would support a Peter Costello-style baby bonus to incentivise Australians to have children, Hastie said he was “pretty open minded”.

The Liberal MP noted there were mixed views on whether the baby bonus among economists but he said he would “support anything that allows young Australians to form families soon enough”.

Hastie said:

I have three kids myself, they are a great blessing, I love children. I’d love other Australians to have kids as well, and part of the challenge is getting them into homes sooner and making the economy work for them.

  • A cool change swept across much of the east cost after an unseasonably warm weekend.

NSW Greens urge government to invest $200m in frontline services after alleged domestic violence incidents

The New South Wales Greens MP Abigail Boyd has urged the state government to invest more in frontline domestic and family violence services after a horror weekend of alleged domestic violence.

Boyd has called for an immediate increase in funding of a minimum $200 million investment to address what she described as “chronic funding shortfalls … causing calls to go unanswered”.

In a statement, Boyd, the Greens’ spokesperson for gendered violence and abuse, said:

Services are operating at up to nine times their funded capacity and waitlists are at an average of two months with some stretching for months on end.

Whenever we see cases like the ones we saw over the weekend, politicians wring their hands and express their sadness as though they have no power to prevent these tragedies from happening.

These issues are not new, nor are the solutions to solve them. Reports, studies, testimony and evidence have all demonstrated for years where the shortfall is and how to address it.

In a $135 billion annual state budget, even if funding was increased, it would still add up to less than half a percent of total annual expenditure. I think most people in NSW would think that’s a small price to pay to prevent these horrific crimes.

Her call comes after police earlier today said they would allege a mother was responsible for Sunday’s stabbing attack on three young children that left one dead and two others fighting for their lives in hospital.

Bystanders were first on the scene after finding the three children and the woman with stab wounds inside a vehicle at Valley Heights in the Blue Mountains, west of Sydney, yesterday afternoon.

On Saturday, three women were allegedly murdered inside their homes within a 12-hour period, in three separate incidents across the state.

Sarah Hanson-Young says telcos can’t be trusted with triple zero

The Greens senator Sarah Hanson-Young has said Australia’s telecommunications system is “failing”, after an inquiry into problems in the sector recommended the government consider nationalising triple zero.

The Senate committee, which delivered its report earlier today, began the inquiry into the Optus triple zero service outage of 18 September 2025, which has been linked to multiple deaths.

The inquiry, which was expanded to cover problems with other telcos including Telstra, which experienced its own outage in July this year, resulted in 11 recommendations to overhaul the system.

Speaking after the report was delivered, Hanson-Young said:

Australia’s telecommunications system is failing and it’s failing because for too long these big corporations have been able to regulate themselves and yet they are essential services.

People should be able to know that they need to call triple zero, their mobile phone will work regardless of where in Australia they are.

One of the key recommendations is urging the government to look at nationalising triple zero.

At the moment it’s a service that is managed by Telstra with support from the other telcos. These companies are not putting the safety of Australians first. They’re putting their profits first and they can no longer be trusted with Australia’s vital triple zero service.

Catie McLeod

Hello, I hope you’ve been having a nice day. I’ll take you through the rest of the news this afternoon.

Nick Visser

That’s all from me. Catie McLeod will take things from here. Take care.

Asic begins proceedings against former CEO of company behind Supercheap Auto, Rebel and Macpac

The Australian Securities and Investments Commission (Asic) has begun civil penalty proceedings against the former CEO and managing director of the Super Retail Group, alleging he breached his duties and provided misleading information to the board and the market.

Asic alleges Anthony Heraghty failed to disclose conflicts of interest that arose from an alleged undisclosed relationship with a senior executive at the company. Those failures, Asic says, included continuing to supervise the person and making decisions affecting their employment, including remuneration, rewards and a redundancy package.

Super Retail Group is an ASX-listed public company and the parent company of a group that has retail interest including Supercheap Auto, BCF, Rebel and Macpac. Heraghty was the CEO from March 2019 to September 2025.

Sarah Court, the chair of Asic, said in a statement:

The allegations in this matter raise important issues about governance, transparency and trust in the information provided to boards and the market.

This case is not about private relationships, but whether a director properly disclosed and managed conflicts of interest and met their duties to the company and shareholders.

Asic is seeking declarations of contravention, pecuniary penalties and disqualification orders. Heraghty has not yet filed a defence, according to The Sydney Morning Herald.

ACT offers $500,000 reward to help solve murder cases including possible Ivan Milat victim

The ACT government will offer a reward of $500,000 for information that helps conclude a series of unsolved murder or missing person cases, including the death of Keren Rowland, a 20-year-old nurse killed in 1971 whose family believe she was the first victim of serial killer Ivan Milat.

The government said the rewards will apply to five new cases in addition to three others that have had rewards attached to them since 2012. Officials said while some of the cases relate to long-term missing persons, they hope the rewards will encourage a witness or someone with information to come forward.

The other cases include those of Elizabeth Herfort, who was last seen in 1980; Megan Louise Mulquiney, last seen in 1984; Troy Hugh Forsyth, who was fatally struck by a van in 1987; and David Abuoi, who was last seen in Canberra in 2012.

The ACT minister for police, Marisa Paterson, said in a statement:

The families of these five people have never given up hope of getting answers regarding what happened to their loved ones. Half a million dollars is a strong incentive for someone to tell police what they know.

If you know anything about Keren, Troy, David, Elizabeth or Megan’s matters, we are urging you to come forward.

Chalmers says AI will bring ‘the biggest economic transformation of our lifetime’

Achol Arok

The treasurer, Jim Chalmers, said artificial intelligence will play “a pivotal role” in driving Australia’s long-term productivity growth.

The AI revolution is the most consequential new emphasis since the 2023 report and the biggest economic transformation of our lifetime. The productivity, investment and labour market impacts of AI will be dramatic.

The IGR shows from 2030 onwards each extra 0.1% of productivity growth from AI could improve the bottom line by 0.7 percentage points and reduce gross debt by 0.3 percentage points within a decade.

Chalmers said Australia needs to be focused and deliberate in adopting AI to realise its benefits.

We are well positioned with Australians adopting AI at a higher rate than almost every G20 country, but the productivity boost from AI depends on translating that into better ways of working.

Achol Arok

More from the treasurer’s response to intergenerational report

Jim Chalmers outlined the five major challenges identified in the intergenerational report:

  • The impact of the “AI revolution” on the economy

  • A “fragmenting world” shaped by growing geopolitical tensions

  • The transition to clean energy

  • A growing and ageing population, accelerated by falling fertility rates

  • Changes to the industrial sector, driven by AI and the energy transition

Chalmers said the challenges needed to be addressed through a holistic approach:

There’s no separating these five accelerating shifts from each other or from their consequences for our budget or our economy.

A smaller workforce means a proportionately smaller income tax base at a time when pressures on social services and tools of statecraft, including defence, will be growing, not easing, along with the fiscal risks of climate change and more frequent disasters.

Chalmers said it was “remarkable” that the budget was strengthening despite those pressures, with government spending over the next 40 years expected to increase by significantly less than previously forecast.

Tasmanian jumping castle tragedy wind gust ‘unprecedented’, inquest hears

A jumping castle that became airborne due to a freak “dust devil”, killing six primary schoolchildren, was tethered at only four of eight anchorage points, an inquest has been told.

The children died during end-of-year celebrations at Hillcrest primary school in Devonport on 16 December 2021.

A long-awaited inquest began in Tasmania on Monday after years of delays due to criminal proceedings against the castle’s operator, Rosemary Gamble. Gamble operated Taz-Zorb, which set up inflatable equipment at the school. She was found not guilty of criminal workplace health and safety breaches in 2025.

The events of the day and the tethering of the castle and other devices would be placed under “extensive examination”, counsel assisting the coroner Maree Norton said on Monday.

Gamble was supervising on the day and had a policy of not operating the castle if winds were tipped to exceed 25km/h. The Bureau of Meteorology forecast for 16 December was light winds, reaching 15 to 20km/h by the evening, Norton said.

Several witnesses, including teachers and nearby residents, said the morning was largely windless before a “mini-tornado” hit around 10am.

In 2025, the magistrates court found Gamble could have taken further steps in relation to the castle’s anchorage, but even if she had, it would have made no difference to the outcome. The coroner can make different findings but cannot make rulings of criminal guilt.

– AAP

Chalmers says intergenerational report warns of ‘very serious risks and pressures’

Achol Arok

The treasurer, Jim Chalmers, has delivered the Treasury’s latest intergenerational report, examining the potential impact of government policies over the next 40 years.

Speaking in Canberra, Chalmers said the report highlighted the challenges facing Australians in a “more fragmented and uncertain world”.

The world is becoming more dangerous, more unpredictable, more unequal, and more divided. And these aren’t just individual threads, they’re part of a bigger fraying of that intergenerational promise of better times.

Accelerating change is putting more pressure on people. It’s eroding trust in the institutions of democracy. It exacerbates the strain felt by younger Australians and younger generations in particular.

Chalmers said the report identified that Australia faces serious challenges but said the country is well prepared to manage them.

This intergenerational report shows that we face very serious risks and pressures, but that we are better placed and better prepared for them … this report also shows that we have a better plan to maximise our opportunities and minimise our risks, to grow our economy and lift living standards, embrace new technologies and share the benefits.

‘That’s nuts’: Queensland premier slams plans to slash visa numbers

Andrew Messenger

Queensland’s premier says bipartisan plans to reduce the number of foreign visa holders allowed into the country is “nuts” and could risk spiralling food prices and damage to regional communities.

Labor, the Liberals and One Nation have all recently released plans to cap or slash migration. Last week the home affairs minister, Tony Burke, released a plan to slash net overseas migration from 292,000 this year to just 225,000 in 2027-28.

“I think that’s nuts,” David Crisafulli said on Monday, referring to the idea of reducing visa numbers year on year. He said:

Without it [migration], you go into a country town during a fruit picking season, for example, and without those short-term visas, you won’t get a beer at a pub, and a farmer won’t be able to pick his or her produce, and those towns grind to a halt.

But if you don’t love those little towns as much as I do, see it through a self-interest point of view. The things you put in your trolley are going to be a hell of a lot more expensive if there’s not a sensible discussion around making sure that people can go into regional areas and do the kind of work that they have done for a long period of time.

Crisafulli said the country needed a discussion as much about welcoming new Australians who wanted to build the country of the future as about how best to accommodate them.

Donna Lu

Four Australian sea lions test positive for H5 bird flu in South Australia

Four more endangered Australian sea lions have tested positive for the deadly H5N1 bird flu at an important breeding site in South Australia.

The animals, including one pup, were among several found dead on the Pages islands near Kangaroo Island, state authorities said on Monday.

SA recorded the first H5 death of a sea lion eight days ago, with fears about how deadly virus will impact populations of the endangered pinniped.

Experts estimate that about 12,000 Australian sea lions remain, most of which are found in SA. The Pages islands are one of three sites in the state with large breeding colonies, according to Parks SA.

Authorities identified three positive sea lions on North Page Island and one on South Page Island via aerial wildlife surveillance operations. Several dead pups were also found, but tested negative for H5 bird flu.

Invasive Species Council chief executive Jack Gough said:

We haven’t seen the mass deaths in pinnipeds that the experience in South America and Antarctica suggests may be coming but multiple deaths in a single location could indicate that devastation is just around the corner.

We’re now about to see millions of migratory birds arriving in Australia as part of spring migration as well as breeding events around the country which could be a new phase in terms of the level of devastation.

WA government calls off shark catch-and-kill directive

The WA government has called off the search for a shark that killed a Perth man on Friday, after a minister had ordered a catch-and-kill directive.

WA police said a 63-year-old man was bitten by a shark while swimming at Sorrento beach. The swimmer’s body has not been found.

In a statement, the Department of Primary Industries said it had concluded water and land based patrols around Sorrento beach.

There was no evidence of white shark activity in the area yesterday and a significantly diminished chance of catching the individual shark involved in the fatal incident on Friday.

Beaches in the City of Joondalup from Marmion to Iluka were set to reopen at 10am local time.

On Saturday the WA fisheries minister, Jackie Jarvis, revealed she had greenlit the order. She said in a social media post:

Given the shark had been positively identified, remained in the vicinity following a fatal attack and was considered to pose an ongoing threat, I authorised fisheries officers to destroy the shark if captured.

More Australians forecast to live into their 90s

Australian households are expected to shrink but more people can expect to live well into their 90s, according to the latest update to forecasts of the country’s long-term future.

Treasury’s latest intergenerational report, to be published in full on Monday, will project the impact of government policies 40 years into the future.

An extract released on Sunday showed life expectancy at birth was forecast to reach almost 90 for women by 2065-66, up from about 86 years at present.

The report will also reveal that artificial intelligence (AI) will become the “defining influence” on the economy over the next four decades, as the treasurer, Jim Chalmers, warned it would come with “very substantial risks”.

Read more:

Andrew Messenger

More than 800,000 bees stolen across far north Queensland

An estimated 800,000 bees, worth tens of thousands of dollars, have been stolen from properties in far north Queensland.

The industry is already reeling from the this month’s arrival of the varroa mite parasite.

Tom Bidner, an apiarist from the Atherton Tablelands, west of Cairns, said 44 colonies had been stolen from three different beekeepers.

Australian diplomats to meet Palestinian counterparts in coming months

Tom McIlroy

Foreign minister Penny Wong has spoken with her Palestinian counterpart, Varsen Aghabekian. The pair agreed that senior officials from both governments should meet in coming months to strengthen bilateral relations and discuss key priorities.

The pair spoke on Friday night, with Aghabekian briefing Wong on progress on the Palestinian Authority’s reform commitments.

“Australia is committed to a two-state solution,” Wong wrote on social media on Monday.

I spoke with Palestinian Foreign Minister, Dr Varsen Aghabekian, about the PA’s reform agenda and our joint efforts to strengthen Palestine’s institutional foundations.

We also discussed the devastating situation in Gaza. “I reiterated that Hamas must play no role in the State of Palestine.

The pair agreed that Israel must halt its illegal settlement activity and hold perpetrators of settler violence to account.

Wong also told Aghabekian that Australia continues to press all parties to implement the Gaza peace plan in full and facilitate unimpeded humanitarian access to Gaza.
